H_hierarchical.evidence: The Planner has explicit multi-level nesting: main -> generate-plan/modify-plan; generate-plan -> old-plan/take-off/main-mission/approach; main-mission -> plan-sequencing/actions-definition/plan-optimization.

G_guards_arith.evidence: Meaningful guards include no selected Flight Plan, final Park appended, Mission Start Time reached, position reached, take-off speed reached, 15m clearance, desired altitude, destination distance, time limit, and ground contact.

A_actions_nontrivial.evidence: The Planner copies executed old-plan parts, appends Actions, sends Flight Plans, and the Execution agent outputs planner feedback, action details, direct/autopilot/payload commands, while verifying action completion.

F_fault_recovery.evidence: The New Plan Trigger can cause cancellation and regeneration of the current Flight Plan while preserving executed parts; scenarios show current Travel aborted/diverted after changed priority, with threats/faults mentioned as replanning causes.

T1_cross_section_element.evidence: Relevant semantics are split across sections: Objective/Action abstractions in §III, Planner hierarchy in §IV, simulation replanning behavior in §V, and Execution command/completion behavior in §VI.

T2_implicit_domain_term.evidence: Terms such as situational awareness, New Plan Trigger, airframe faults, Autopilot, and Commitment to an Objective imply domain-specific replanning and control semantics beyond explicit transition rules.

T3_implicit_action_from_prose.evidence: Action types are tabulated earlier, while concrete effects and completion criteria for parking, taxi, take-off, climb, travel, recon, circle, descent, and landing are narrated later in prose.

T4_multivar_arith_guard.evidence: The paper gives many threshold and high-level predicate conditions, but does not spell out an explicit arithmetic or boolean guard formula over multiple variables.

T5_composite_internal_behavior.evidence: Composite states are decomposed into sub-states, but the paper does not clearly specify parent entry/during/exit behavior independent of child-state behavior.

T6_global_cross_cutting_recovery.evidence: The paper states that replanning can occur at any moment; the trigger cancels/regenerates the plan and can make execution divert from the current action, a cross-cutting rule over many action states.

C1_speculative_dfs.evidence: The Planner has a deep composite chain with conditional top-level routing into generate-plan versus modify-plan and ordered descent through nested generation phases.

C2_expr_ir_smt.evidence: No sufficiently explicit arithmetic/boolean guard set is present for SMT-style consistency checking.

C3_forced_and_aspect.evidence: The replanning/diversion rule can apply across many execution action types; a forced transition or parent-level monitor would avoid duplicating the same trigger across each action state.

C4_abstract_action.evidence: The architecture uses abstract Actions and generic payload/autopilot command layers, but many Execution actions are still mapped to concrete speed, pitch, roll, yaw, brake, waypoint, or payload commands.

key_nl_quotes: Planner agent can be described by ten states and sub-states
replanning can occur at any moment
one_line_pitch: This is a strong stress test because it combines deep Planner hierarchy, cross-section action attribution, non-trivial command outputs, and a global replanning/diversion rule over many UAV mission actions.
rationale: The sample is fundamentally hierarchical and action-heavy, with the Planner and Execution agents jointly defining a real mission-management supervisor rather than a toy FSM. Its weakest-baseline pressure comes from split semantics, implicit UAV planning terminology, and a cross-cutting replanning trigger that prior Umple/PlantUML-style baselines would likely flatten or duplicate incorrectly. Guard formulas are not mathematically rich, but the volume of completion predicates and command side effects still makes it a strong top-set candidate.
